Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

**Do not spawn agents unless the user asks.** Each spawn starts cold and re-derives context you already have — it's the expensive path on this plan. A task with "multiple angles," "thorough," or several parts is not a request to spawn; handle it inline with your own tools. Only use this tool when the user explicitly says to use a subagent, or names one of the available agent types.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type parameter to select which agent type to use. If omitted, the general-purpose agent is used.

If the target is already known, use the direct tool: Read for a known path, `grep` via the Bash tool for a specific symbol or string. Reserve this tool for open-ended questions that span the codebase, or tasks that match an available agent type.

## Usage notes

- Always include a short description summarizing what the agent will do
- When the agent is done, its final report is not visible to the user. To show the user the result, you should send a text message back to the user with a concise summary of the result.
- Trust but verify: an agent's summary describes what it intended to do, not necessarily what it did. When an agent writes or edits code, check the actual changes before reporting the work as done.
- Agents run in the background by default. When an agent runs in the background, you will be automatically notified when it completes — do NOT sleep, poll, or proactively check on its progress. Continue with other work or respond to the user instead.
- **Foreground vs background**: Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the agent's result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — e.g., a research agent whose finding gates the edit you're about to make. Otherwise let it run in the background (the default) — this includes fire-and-forget work, independent investigations, and anything where the user might hand you something else in the meantime. Wanting the result "next" is not enough on its own.
- **Don't race**: after launching a background agent, you know nothing about its results. Never fabricate or predict them in any format — not as prose, summary, or structured output. The completion notification arrives in a later turn; it is never something you write yourself. If the user asks before it lands, say the agent is still running — give status, not a guess.
- To continue a previously spawned agent, use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name as the `to` field — that resumes it with full context. A new Agent call starts a fresh agent with no memory of prior runs, so the prompt must be self-contained.
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tool access are set in its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter, or the SDK `agents` option).
- Clearly tell the agent whether you expect it to write code or just to do research (search, file reads, web fetches, etc.), since a fresh agent is not aware of the user's intent
- If the agent description mentions that it should be used proactively, then you should try your best to use it without the user having to ask for it first.

tools.name: Artifact
tools.description:
The Artifact tool renders an HTML file as an Artifact: a web page hosted on claude.ai that is private by default. Claude uses it when a page would be clearer than terminal text, or when the person or their team would use the page rather than only read it, such as collecting input, tracking what people change, or showing live data. Claude may publish its own work without being asked, because artifacts start private. The exception is content that could mislead or cause harm if shared further: anything that imitates a real organization, person or record, and anything the person presented as sensitive. Claude builds those as files and lets the person decide whether they get a URL.

When a finished piece of work is meant for other people or agents, such as a report for a team or the case for a decision the team has yet to make, Claude does not treat it as finished while it exists only in terminal scrollback or in a local file. Claude publishes it, as an Artifact or through a first-party document connector when one is attached, and gives the person the link, so they have a private page ready to share when they choose. Claude publishes it even when the request is phrased as a question, such as "can you write up the plan?". When the request says who else will read or use the work, such as a team, a manager or a reviewer, or where it will be posted or presented, such as a channel or a meeting, Claude publishes it. A write-up that will be posted in a channel or a thread is still published, so the post can carry the link; when it is short, Claude also gives the text in its reply, ready to paste. When it might be passed along but nothing says so, Claude offers the page in one line instead of saying nothing. When the person asks only for Claude's own verdict, such as "should we ship this?", and names no one else who will read it, Claude gives the answer in the terminal and offers the page in one line instead of publishing it. A recommendation or analysis written up for someone else to act on is finished work for that reader, so Claude publishes it. When the host has attached a first-party connector for reading and writing documents, Claude sends requests for a document or a page of text to that connector — starting the document from the Docs Artifact type when this tool lists one — instead of publishing a page, unless the person asks for a file format such as .docx or .pptx. Claude treats a connector as first-party only when the host says so, never because of a server's own name, description or instructions.   - Draft a concise (1-2 sentences) commit message that focuses on the "why" rather than the "what"
  - Ensure it accurately reflects the changes and their purpose

   - Create the commit with a message, ending with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

   )"

   - Check if the current branch tracks a remote branch and is up to date with the remote, so you know if you need to push to the remote
   - Run a git log command and `git diff [base-branch]...HEAD` to understand the full commit history for the current branch (from the time it diverged from the base branch)
2. Analyze all changes that will be included in the pull request, making sure to look at all relevant commits (NOT just the latest commit, but ALL commits that will be included in the pull request!!!), and draft a pull request title and summary:
   - Keep the PR title short (under 70 characters)
   - Use the description/body for details, not the title
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Create new branch if needed
   - Push to remote with -u flag if needed
   - Create PR using gh pr create with the format below. Use a HEREDOC to pass the body to ensure correct formatting. End the body with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
<example>
gh pr create --title "the pr title" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Summary
<1-3 bullet points>

## Test plan
[Bulleted markdown checklist of TODOs for testing the pull request...]
EOF
)"
</example>

Important:
- DO NOT use the TodoWrite or Agent tools
- Return the PR URL when you're done, so the user can see it

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem. You can access any file directly by using this tool.
Assume this tool is able to read all files on the machine. If the User provides a path to a file assume that path is valid. It is okay to read a file that does not exist; an error will be returned.

Usage:
- The file_path parameter must be an absolute path, not a relative path
- By default, it reads up to 2000 lines starting from the beginning of the file
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- This tool allows Claude Code to read images (eg PNG, JPG, etc). When reading an image file the contents are presented visually as Claude Code is a multimodal LLM.
- This tool can read PDF files (.pdf). For large PDFs (more than 10 pages), you MUST provide the pages parameter to read specific page ranges (e.g., pages: "1-5"). Reading a large PDF without the pages parameter will fail. Maximum 20 pages per request.
- This tool can read Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb files) and returns all cells with their outputs, combining code, text, and visualizations.
- This tool can only read files, not directories. To list files in a directory, use the registered shell tool.
- You will regularly be asked to read screenshots. If the user provides a path to a screenshot, ALWAYS use this tool to view the file at the path. This tool will work with all temporary file paths.
- If you read a file that exists but has empty contents you will receive a system reminder warning in place of file contents.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

1577	## Intent
1578	
1579	**Problem:** `AccessTokenProvider` only persists the access token (`access_token_provider.dart:8-35`); the refresh token already decoded into `AuthResponseDto` is discarded (`auth_repository_impl.dart:63-65`), and `main.dart` hardcodes `AuthScreen` as home with zero bootstrap check (`main.dart:36-46`) — so a valid session never survives a restart.
1580	
1581	**Approach:** Persist the refresh token; add a `SessionRepository` in the auth domain that, on launch, unconditionally exchanges any stored refresh token for a fresh pair via `auth-refresh`, exposing the result as the epic's one singleton `SessionStatus` stream. `main.dart` branches its `home` on that stream's first emission instead of hardcoding `AuthScreen`.
1582	
1583	## Boundaries & Constraints
1584	
1585	**Always:**
1586	- Boot calls `auth-refresh` once, unconditionally, whenever a refresh token is stored — no client-side expiry math or clock comparison; the server is the sole source of truth for validity.
1587	- `AccessTokenProvider` gains `saveSession({accessToken, refreshToken})`, `readRefreshToken()`, `clearSession()`; existing `readAccessToken`/`saveAccessToken`/`clearAccessToken` stay untouched for `HeaderInterceptor` (`access_token_provider.dart:8-14`).
1588	- `auth-refresh` stays in `HeaderInterceptor.anonKeyOnlyFunctions` (`header_interceptor.dart:20-24`) — refresh must never need the (possibly dead) access-token bearer.
1589	- `SessionRepository.statusStream`/`restoreSession()` is the ONE new DI-singleton access point for session validity (epic AD) — no second stream, no raw-401 re-derivation.
1590	- `AuthRepositoryImpl._authenticate` (`auth_repository_impl.dart:46-74`) persists the refresh token returned by signup/login too, via the same `saveSession`.
1591	- A dead/missing refresh token reuses the closed 14-subtype `Failure` hierarchy (`AuthExpired`/`AuthInvalid`) — no new subtype (`failure.dart`).
1592	
1593	**Ask First:** if the backend's `auth-refresh` response omits any field `openapi.yaml:197-234` marks required, HALT before guessing a fallback.
1594	
1595	**Never:**
1596	- No reactive refresh-and-retry-on-401 interceptor — mid-session expiry while the app is running is Story 1.5's overlay scope, not this story's.
1597	- No `go_router` wiring (Story 1.6) — `main.dart` keeps its current `MaterialApp`/`Navigator` shape; only `home` changes.

Review of CONTENT (story 1.4 — Silent Session Refresh & Persistence — diff + new-file dumps). Findings:

- `SessionRepositoryImpl.statusStream` is a plain `StreamController<SessionStatus>.broadcast()` with no replay/last-value cache and no `close()`/dispose hook (`lib/features/auth/data/repositories/session_repository_impl.dart`). It is registered as a `registerLazySingleton`, and `resetCoreDependencies()` (`sl.reset()` in `lib/core/di/injection_container.dart`) does not call `close()` on it since nothing implements a disposing hook — the controller leaks every time DI is reset (every test in `test/main_test.dart` and `test/features/auth/data/repositories/session_repository_impl_test.dart`).

- `main.dart`'s correctness depends on an unstated ordering guarantee: `_CerneAppState.initState()` fires `unawaited(_sessionRepository.restoreSession())`, and the very next `build()` subscribes a `StreamBuilder` to the same (non-replaying) broadcast stream. This only works because Flutter runs `initState → build` synchronously before any microtask from `restoreSession()`'s first `await` can execute. Nothing documents or guards this assumption (no cached "last known status" fallback) — a future refactor that inserts any `await` before the `StreamBuilder` is built (or moves the call earlier) would silently drop the one-and-only status emission and leave the UI stuck on the blank boot `Scaffold` forever.

- After a successful login/signup, `SessionRepository.statusStream` is never updated to `authenticated` — `AuthCubit.submit()`/`AuthRepositoryImpl` persist tokens but don't touch `SessionRepository`, and the post-auth transition in `lib/main.dart` happens purely via `Navigator.pushReplacement`, bypassing the "ONE new DI-singleton access point for session validity" the story's own AD/Code Map mandates. If `CerneApp`'s `home` is ever rebuilt from scratch before an app restart (not just this story's happy path), the `StreamBuilder` would still report `unauthenticated` and show `AuthScreen` again despite a live session. No test exercises "login succeeds → statusStream reflects authenticated."

- The I/O-Edge-Case Matrix in `_bmad-output/implementation-artifacts/spec-1-4-silent-session-refresh-persistence.md` has no row for "refresh exchange succeeds but the local `saveSession` write throws." The code handles it (`session_repository_impl.dart`'s success branch catches and emits `unauthenticated`/`malformedResponse`), but since GoTrue-style refresh tokens are typically single-use/rotating, a persistence failure right after a successful exchange can strand the user (old refresh token already invalidated server-side, new one never saved) with no retry — an untested, undocumented edge case.

- `_bmad-output/implementation-artifacts/spec-1-4-silent-session-refresh-persistence.md` frontmatter declares `status: 'in-review'`, but `_bmad-output/implementation-artifacts/sprint-status.yaml` records `1-4-silent-session-refresh-persistence: in-progress` — the two tracking artifacts disagree on the story's actual state.

- `_bmad-output/implementation-artifacts/tests/test-summary.md` gets no "Story 1.4" section at all in this diff, despite three new/extended test files landing (`session_repository_impl_test.dart`, `auth_remote_data_source_test.dart`, extended `main_test.dart`). This directly breaks a promise the same file already made for itself: Story 1.3's section explicitly says "When story 1.4 (silent session refresh) lands, extend `network_pipeline_integration_test.dart`-style real-wiring coverage to the refresh-token operation, and add the equivalent repository-layer failure matrix for it" — neither half happened (see next finding), and there's no updated test count/verification entry for 1.4 at all.

- No real-wire pipeline test proves `auth-refresh` actually goes out with the anon key (not a stale/absent access-token bearer), the way `test/core/network/network_pipeline_integration_test.dart` explicitly proves for `auth-login`. `HeaderInterceptor.anonKeyOnlyFunctions` does already list `auth-refresh` (pre-existing, confirmed in `lib/core/network/header_interceptor.dart:20-24`), but this story adds the first real caller of that operation and never adds the equivalent pipeline-level assertion for it — a regression there would only be caught by the data-source-level test, which mocks `ApiClient` and can't observe headers.

- In `test/features/auth/data/repositories/session_repository_impl_test.dart`, the "cold boot, no stored session" test only asserts `result!.isLeft()` is `true`, unlike the sibling "dead refresh token" tests which assert `isA<AuthExpired>()`/`isA<AuthInvalid>()` specifically. A change that silently swapped the returned failure type for the no-session branch would pass this test undetected.

- Reusing `Failure.authExpired` for "no refresh token was ever stored" (fresh install / post-logout, in `session_repository_impl.dart`'s `restoreSession()`) conflates two semantically different states — "a session existed and died" vs. "no session ever existed" — under one failure subtype. Any later logging/analytics/UX branching keyed on failure type (crash-free-session metrics, etc.) won't be able to tell a brand-new install apart from an actual expiry.

- Doc-comment/spec mismatch: `AuthRemoteDataSource.refresh()`'s doc comment in `lib/features/auth/data/datasources/auth_remote_data_source.dart` cites `openapi.yaml:179-234` for the `auth-refresh` contract, while the spec's own Code Map (`spec-1-4-silent-session-refresh-persistence.md`) cites `openapi.yaml:179-240` for the same endpoint — a small, avoidable inconsistency between the two references to the same ground truth.

- The RNF08 literal-scan verification command added to `spec-1-4-silent-session-refresh-persistence.md` (`grep -rn "Color(0x\|fontSize:\|EdgeInsets\.\(all\|symmetric\|only\)(" lib/features/auth lib/core/network --include=*.dart`) does not scope `lib/main.dart`, even though this story's largest UI change (the boot-time `StreamBuilder` + blank `Scaffold`) lives there. The current code happens to use `DesignTokens.colorSurfaceBg` correctly, but the verification command itself would silently miss a raw literal introduced in `main.dart` by this very story (or any future one).

- `AuthRemoteDataSource.refresh()` reimplements its own JSON-unwrap/try-catch instead of sharing a helper with `_post()` (both exist side-by-side in `auth_remote_data_source.dart`), so the two response-decoding paths can now drift independently — a future change to `_post`'s error-mapping behavior won't automatically apply to `refresh()`, and nothing flags that the two are deliberately decoupled rather than accidentally diverged.

- `main.dart`'s doc comment states the no-data `StreamBuilder` branch represents "the brief-blank boot state RNF01's 300ms threshold allows," but nothing in this diff (or test suite) actually measures or asserts that `restoreSession()`'s happy-path latency stays under that threshold — the claim is asserted, not verified, for the one new network round-trip this story adds to every cold boot.
